variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external context and capabilities. It standardizes how an application discovers and uses server-provided resources, prompts, and tools over JSON-RPC instead of building a different connector contract for every integration.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Choose the primitive that matches the owner of the action”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Resources
pairs.detail: Addressable context such as files, schemas, or records.
pairs.explanation: Addressable context such as files, schemas, or records. The client lists or reads a URI, validates it, and decides whether to place the result in model context.

pairs.label: Prompts
pairs.explanation: Reusable message templates or workflows. A user explicitly chooses a prompt, and the client retrieves its arguments and messages.

pairs.label: Tools
pairs.detail: Schema-described functions that the model may request.
pairs.explanation: Schema-described functions that the model may request. The host intercepts the request, shows the inputs, applies policy, obtains user consent, and can deny execution.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. The core invariant is capability is not authority.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Resources: Addressable context such as files, schemas, or records. Prompts: Reusable message templates or workflows. Tools: Schema-described functions that the model may request.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Complete the lifecycle before normal operations”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Propose a version
pairs.detail: The client sends initialize with its latest supported protocol version, client information, and client capabilities.
pairs.explanation: The client sends initialize with its latest supported protocol version, client information, and client capabilities.

pairs.label: Negotiate support
pairs.detail: The server returns a version it supports, its implementation information, and server capabilities.
pairs.explanation: The server returns a version it supports, its implementation information, and server capabilities. The client disconnects if it cannot support the result.

pairs.label: Mark the session ready
pairs.explanation: The client sends notifications/initialized. Before this point, normal tools, resources, and prompts requests should not begin.

pairs.label: Operate within the contract
pairs.detail: Each side respects the negotiated version and capabilities, applies local policy, enforces timeouts, and shuts down through the transport.
pairs.explanation: Each side respects the negotiated version and capabilities, applies local policy, enforces timeouts, and shuts down through the transport.

variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Propose a version: The client sends initialize with its latest supported protocol version, client information, and client capabilities. Negotiate support: The server returns a version it supports, its implementation information, and server capabilities. Mark the session ready: The client sends notifications/initialized. Operate within the contract: Each side respects the negotiated version and capabilities, applies local policy, enforces timeouts, and shuts down through the transport.

variants.prompt: From the lesson section “Select transport by process boundary”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: stdio
pairs.detail: The client launches a server and exchanges newline-delimited messages over standard input and output.
pairs.explanation: The client launches a server and exchanges newline-delimited messages over standard input and output. Keep logs on standard error, pin the executable, constrain its environment, and sandbox filesystem and network access.

pairs.label: Streamable HTTP
pairs.detail: The server exposes one MCP endpoint using HTTP POST and GET, with optional server-sent events.
pairs.explanation: The server exposes one MCP endpoint using HTTP POST and GET, with optional server-sent events. Validate Origin, authenticate every request, bind only to localhost for local-only service, and support both JSON and event-stream responses.

pairs.label: Protocol contract
pairs.detail: Pin supported revisions, test initialization order, validate schemas, honor negotiated sub-capabilities, and distinguish requests from notifications.
pairs.explanation: Pin supported revisions, test initialization order, validate schemas, honor negotiated sub-capabilities, and distinguish requests from notifications.

pairs.label: Trust contract
pairs.detail: Verify server provenance, minimize context, audience-bind tokens, separate upstream credentials, and require fresh approval for sensitive effects.
pairs.explanation: Verify server provenance, minimize context, audience-bind tokens, separate upstream credentials, and require fresh approval for sensitive effects.

pairs.label: Operational contract
pairs.detail: Set timeouts, cancellation and reconciliation rules, idempotency boundaries, session expiry behavior, audit evidence, and revocation paths.
pairs.explanation: Set timeouts, cancellation and reconciliation rules, idempotency boundaries, session expiry behavior, audit evidence, and revocation paths.

variants.prompt: What does successful MCP capability negotiation establish?
options: The client and server support specific protocol features for this session.
The server is trusted to execute every advertised tool.
The user has approved every future side effect.
Every tool annotation is accurate.
variants.explanation: Capabilities establish protocol support. Trust, authorization, exposure, and user approval remain separate host and server decisions.

variants.prompt: Why must an MCP proxy use a separate token for a downstream API?
options: The inbound token is audience-bound to the MCP server, and token passthrough is forbidden.
MCP access tokens cannot be sent in HTTP headers.
Downstream APIs must always use anonymous access.
A session ID automatically becomes the downstream credential.
variants.explanation: The MCP server must validate tokens issued for itself and must not pass them through. It acts as a separate OAuth client to its upstream API.

It gives all three servers one shared session and conversation history.

Ask for a broader token scope.
